sentences: For three years, the man has studied eastern magic with the Yogis in a distant country and is now known by his new identity, the magician.
He now has the power to teleport, astral project, mesmerize, as well as project illusions.
With these supernatural abilities he has been entrusted by his teacher to "go forth with his youth and strength to conquer the evil that threatens mankind".
The magician is sent to a desert country to deal with an Egyptian megalomaniac known as the villain.
The villain kidnaps the magician's brother-in-law, the engineer, an inventor who has developed a death ray whose beams reach halfway round the world.
The evil villain plots to use the ray to aid his plans for world domination.

The magician must utilise all his psychic abilities to rescue his brother-in-law, and also his sister and their children, whom the villain has kidnapped in a plot to force the engineer into revealing the secrets of his death ray.
The magician's sweetheart the Egyptian princess is also kidnapped, leaving the magician with the quandary whom to rescue first.
Using his Yogi abilities, the magician makes daring escapes, including one from a submerged sarcophagus.
Eventually he succeeds in rescuing everyone and mesmerizing the villain long enough to destroy both the death ray and the villain's entire lair.
During the filming of a death scene of the film, leading man the actor is really shot and killed.
The film studio manager the executive is assigned to handle the situation.

The studio wants to pass it off as a simple accident, but screenwriter the writer digs a bullet out of a wall and tells Homicide Detective the lieutenant that it is a.38 caliber, while the guns used in the film are all.45s.

The lieutenant finds a letter in the dead man's pocket, in which the actor wrote to his lawyer that the actress, his co-star and ex-wife, would not sign a release as beneficiary of his $200,000 life insurance policy.

The bit player, an alcoholic extra with a self-admitted grudge against the actor for getting him fired as head gaffer (electrician), is spotted trying to dispose of a loaded.38, but the writer points out that the gun has not been fired.
The writer suggests they view the footage of the fatal scene for clues, but somebody knocks out the projectionist and burns the print using a cigarette with rouge on it.
It is a special rouge normally used by only two women.
One was away on location, making the actress the prime suspect.
Before another print can be made, the negative is destroyed with acid.
While snooping around on the set, the writer finds a derringer mounted inside a lamp and electrically wired to be fired remotely, but he is knocked out and the gun taken.
He goes to question the bit player, but finds him dead beside a glass of poison and a written confession.
However, the writer finds several clues that make him suspicious.
Through more detective work, he discovers that the new battery of the actress's car is dry, and battery fluid is poisonous.
In the actor's dressing room, the writer finds a letter from a love-stricken married woman named "the letter-writer" and a hotel room key.

Later, in the executive's office, the lieutenant takes the actress into custody; the writer spots a photo of a woman on the desk; the inscription reveals that the executive's wife is named the letter-writer.
When the writer goes to the hotel, he finds out from a bellhop that the actor had been there with a woman; her husband was waiting, and the two men got into a fight.
The studio decides to finish the film (only the last, fatal scene needs to be shot), using a double for the actor and arranging for the actress's temporary release.
The writer finds out from the prop man that the guns were originally supposed to be.38s, but he made an unauthorized substitution.
The writer takes him to the lieutenant.
Just as he is about to reveal who ordered the guns, the lights go out.
(The murderer had overheard the conversation through a studio microphone.)
After a gunfight and chase, the killer falls to his death.
It is the filmmaker, the director.

The wife meets her former boyfriend the old flame at the local aquarium, and asks him for some money so she can leave her husband, stockbroker the financier; but the financier receives an anonymous telephone call tipping him off to the rendezvous.
When he confronts the pair, the old flame knocks him out with a punch.
As no witnesses see the altercation, he hides the unconscious man in the room behind an exhibit.
Schoolteacher the schoolmistress takes her class on a field trip to the aquarium.
She helps stop a pickpocket, the thief, by tripping him with her umbrella, but he slips away.
Soon afterward, she loses her hatpin; one of her students finds it.
Then she sees the financier's corpse falling into a pool housing a penguin.

The police inspector arrives and uncovers several suspects: the widow and the old flame; the curator, the head of the aquarium, who had financial dealings with the deceased; and the thief, found hiding near the scene.
Lawyer the attorney, a bystander, catches the wife when she faints, and acquires a client when she is taken in for questioning.
He also becomes the old flame's lawyer.

The schoolmistress makes herself useful to the inspector by taking notes on his interviews and her observations, typing them up for him, calling attention to points he has missed, and making him a meal.
He is appreciative enough to not object when she continues to insert herself into his investigation.
However, she herself later becomes a suspect when it is determined that her hatpin was driven through the man's right ear into his brain.
The old flame confesses to protect the wife, but the schoolmistress does not believe him.
She convinces the inspector to notify the press that the murder was committed with a thrust through the left ear.
Later, the attorney passes along a message from the thief, in which he claims to know the identity of the killer.
When the inspector and the schoolmistress go to see him at the jail, though, they find him dead from hanging.

The attorney demonstrates a way in which the old flame could have escaped from his nearby cell using a duplicate key (which is found), strangled the thief, and hanged him with wire without entering the thief's cell.
At the murder trial of the old flame and the wife, the attorney questions the schoolmistress, but slips up, showing that he knew that the financier was killed via the right ear.
He phoned the tip to the old flame and killed him because he is the wife's lover and wanted her to himself.
When the wife is released, the waiting old flame slaps her in the face, to the amusement of the inspector and the schoolmistress.
The inspector then unexpectedly asks the schoolmistress to marry him.
(In the sequel, the next film, they are still single.)
Note on sources.
Beautiful courtesan the blackmailer intends to “retire” to another continent, sailing first class and “alone, for once.”

She gathers four rich and powerful former lovers—the rancher, the engaged man, the third lover and the married man—along with the married man's wife and the engaged man's fiancée, for an impromptu weekend party at the rancher's ranch on the western coast.
She blackmails the rancher into hosting the event and informs him that his nephew and heir, the fiancé, is engaged to her young sister, the girl.
The girl and the fiancé arrive at the blackmailer's apartment and decide to go to the ranch, too.
A man named the stranger has been following the blackmailer.
At the ranch house (1804) near the town, the guests are playing darts.
The blackmailer's surprise entrance stuns the three men.
The rancher introduces a mysterious guest.
The rancher's sister, the aunt, arrives unexpectedly, obsessed with the family's old western bloodline and worried about her nephew's engagement.
The thunderstorms begin after dinner.
Alone in the library with her victims, the blackmailer observes that they have all been “gamboling on the same green,” unaware.
She demands money from each man according to his means—$50,000 from the engaged man, $100,000 from the rancher, $25,000 from the third lover and $250,000 from the married man.
The rancher reveals that the guest wants her as his mistress: “I'm through with that,” she replies.
Her maid, the servant, interrupts to give the blackmailer a small box, delivered to the apartment.
It contains a fraternity pin.

Disturbed, the blackmailer tells the four another reason why she is through: Flashback: Three weeks before, in the mountains, an unnamed young man, scion of a wealthy family, gives the blackmailer his fraternity pin, and tells her that he will get no money from his father if he marries before he is 25.
She returns the pin and warns him to “stay away from hungry Mama bears.”
He says “Goodbye” and steps off the cliff...
The married man scoffs—the pin was delivered “from the grave, I suppose.”
The blackmailer goes to her room and throws the pin out into the storm.
She sees the boy's face gleaming in the trees outside.
At 3 a.m., the stranger is prowling downstairs.
The blackmailer screams and staggers from her room, a dart in her neck.
He catches her; she murmurs “That face.”
He puts her body on the sofa and leaves, but a landslide blocks the road.
The house is roused.
The aunt phones the town police but is stopped by the stranger, who introduces himself as the investigator, a big eastern city private detective.
He has teamed up with gangster the mobster (a childhood friend) and the mobster's henchmen to retrieve a client's love letters to the blackmailer.
The investigator starts his own investigation, knowing the police are coming; they will pin the crime on him unless he finds the killer first.
The investigator and the fiancé find the girl unconscious in the blackmailer's room.
She remembers talking to the aunt and going to the blackmailer.
She was clubbed with a candlestick.
The investigator interviews suspects, including the guest, who confesses—that his name is really another name.
The lights go out; a white face appears and disappears.
A distraught guest/father cries out: It is the death mask of his son, the dead youth (the unnamed youth in the blackmailer's story).
He wore it when he knocked out the girl and tried to kill the blackmailer.
The father dies of a heart attack.
“Wait, I remember now!”
The lights go out; she is stabbed with a dart that misses her neck.
The visitor, a mid-life American businessman, arrives at a capital-city hotel for a vacation.
He finds a hotel maid, the chambermaid, in his room unpacking for him.
She offers him some advice about what to wear for dinner at the hotel dining room, where his nervous and clumsy behavior annoys the other guests.
After eating in his room, he tries to chat with the chambermaid, who resists such informality but tells him that he will experience a capital-city foggy night, "a real pea-souper."
Going for a walk, he becomes disoriented and asks for directions to the hotel.
Coming to a door that resembles the hotel's, he rings and knocks with no answer, but finds the door unlatched and enters what appears to be an upper-class house with a large tapestry by the stairs.
No one is immediately present, but he spies someone in an armchair through an open door, who turns out be a man with a bloody head, apparently dead.
When the visitor sees a man fleeing outside, he chases after him but loses him.
A well-dressed man, who identifies himself as the gentleman suggests that they go back to the house to call the police.
At the house, the visitor and the gentleman find the front door locked, and their knock is answered by a butler.
Going in, the visitor confirms that it is the same house when he saw the tapestry, but there is no body in the armchair and the room is occupied by the owners, the major and his wife the hostess.

The householders are at first annoyed and then amused by the brash American's claims to have seen a body, and they are soon joined by their niece the young woman, who was at the theater after having just arrived from a faraway country.
When the householders and the gentleman excuse themselves to call the police, the visitor and the young woman chat, revealing that she has never met her uncle and aunt before.

Going to the room where the visitor and the young woman expect to find the householders calling the police, they instead overhear them complaining to the gentleman that he had not given them enough time to "fix things up."
Shaken, the visitor and the young woman return to the other room to decide what to do when a man with a bandaged head enters.
The visitor immediately recognizes him as the "body" he had seen in the armchair.
The man identifies himself as the bandaged man, a British "secret agent," who had been injured confronting the householders, whom he claims to be imposters and part of an international gang.
The bandaged man asks the couple to go to his superior, a man named the boss, and let him know that the bandaged man is pretending to be dead.

For identification, he gives the visitor a large cigarette case and suggests that the two exit the house through the attic and go across the rooftops to another house where they can safely exit to the street.
On the roof, the visitor and the young woman encounter the thief, a friendly burglar, who agrees to help them escape.
Together, they crash an upper-class party in another house and eventually get to the street and to the address the bandaged man gave them.
These scenes involve a number of humorous situations involving mistaken identity and British class distinctions and diction while demonstrating the young woman's intelligence, humor, and nerve.
Scenes back at the house, meanwhile, reveal that the bandaged man has been blackmailing the householders with letters concealed in the cigarette case.

When the visitor and the young woman meet the boss, they quickly realize that something is wrong, but the boss and his accomplices take them hostage, tying up the visitor and planning to take the young woman to another hideout.
The thief, who had stayed nearby outside, comes into the room where the visitor is tied up and releases him.
The two are able to release the young woman, who had been hidden in a large sack, and the thief takes her place.
The bandaged man arrives at the scene, but the thief (who has been discovered), the visitor, and the young woman are able to make the bandaged man and the boss suspect each other of double-play.
In a struggle, a gun is fired and two policemen arrive to arrest the gang while the visitor, the young woman, and the thief escape out the back way with the incriminating cigarette case.
Outside, the thief looks on wistfully as the visitor suggests marriage to the young woman and the two embrace.
The big city's Police Commissioner the lawman (an actor) decides to take a vacation after six years of fighting crime, accompanied by his attractive secretary, the assistant (an actress).
On the train to their destination, they spot a rundown circus, "the travelling show", heading to the same place.

The circus is home to a love triangle: the aerialist (an actress), her husband the jealous acrobat (an actor) (whom she is intent on divorcing), and her lover the rival acrobat (an actor (actor)), all three trapeze performers.
The publicist (an actor), the circus's press agent, recognizes his old friend the lawman as the circus parades through town and gives him and the assistant free passes.
The aerialist's horse is spooked and runs away with her; the aerialist escapes unharmed.
The publicist takes a reluctant lawman to see the circus owner (an actor) that night.

The circus owner tells him that someone is out to destroy his show; each of the principal performers received an anonymous note telling them not to perform tomorrow - Friday the 13th - or they will die.
He also cites the aerialist's near accident.
The lawman, however, suspects that it is all a publicity stunt concocted by the publicist.

The assistant reveals that the runaway horse was engineered by the jealous acrobat popping a balloon; she also was able to lipread what the jealous acrobat said to his wife just before: "You double-crossing cheat.
I'll kill the both of you."
The circus owner also informs the lawman that the aerialist, the star attraction, owns half the circus.
When they go to see the jealous acrobat, they find a note saying that he is the "first to go", a bullet hole in the window of his wagon and blood on his cot.
However, there is no body, which arouses the lawman's suspicions.
Then the aerialist's beloved dog is found with its throat cut.
As the lawman is questioning the aerialist, someone throws a voodoo doll through her window.
The next day, the assistant reports that the blood is not human.
The lawman surmises that it is dog's blood, and he noticed an extra member of the "cannibal" troupe last night, the jealous acrobat in disguise.
The lawman searches the circus for the madman.
He advises the circus owner to cancel the performance, but the aerialist insists on going on with the show.
Outside, unnoticed, the jealous acrobat climbs to the top of the Big Top tent.
The rival acrobat is nearly killed when one of trapeze ropes gives way, partially cut by the jealous acrobat, but he escapes unscathed.
The audience believes it is all part of his act.
Then the aerialist performs, also on the trapeze.
The jealous acrobat shoots her with a poison dart using a blowgun.
She falls to the ground and dies.
Afterward, when the lawman roams the grounds, he encounters the jealous acrobat, armed with a pistol and holding the assistant captive.
He orders the lawman to see to it that the rival acrobat is alone in the tent with the aerialist's body.
When he sees people leave the tent, he ventures inside with the assistant, then shoots the rival acrobat in the back.
It is actually the lawman in disguise and wearing bulletproof clothing (borrowed from the circus).
The jealous acrobat races into the Big Top to put on his last performance, high in the air.
At the end, he shoots himself.
The first showgirl and the second showgirl are two showgirls living in the resort hotel.
When the second showgirl refuses one of her wealthy male friend's sexual advances, he chooses to let the second showgirl and the first showgirl pay for their own hotel bills.
They decide to ask the former showgirl, who is engaged to millionaire the rich man, for help paying the bills because the former showgirl used to be a fellow showgirl.
However, the former showgirl pretends not to know them.
The first showgirl tries to win some money gambling, but ends up losing all their money instead.

When they run into the former showgirl's former boyfriend the old flame in the hotel, he offers them some money to leave town, but the second showgirl and the first showgirl accidentally miss the train.
Later, the rich man and the former showgirl are married, but the former showgirl goes missing, and a gangster named the hoodlum is found dead in the hotel's garden.
The rich man offers a large reward to the public for any information about the former showgirl.
The first showgirl and the second showgirl decide to find the former showgirl and claim the reward.

After the rich man, the first showgirl, and the second showgirl survive a near fatal car accident, the first showgirl suggests that they wreck the car and declare the rich man dead from the automobile accident.
When the former showgirl returns to the hotel after the rich man's assumed death, she claims that the rich man had drugged and kidnapped her and killed the hoodlum.
However, the first showgirl pulls a gun on the former showgirl and she confesses that she was going to run away with the old flame, and when the hoodlum tried to stop them, the old flame killed him.
The old flame and the former showgirl are arrested by the police, and the rich man gives the reward to the first showgirl.
Later, the rich man decides to marry the second showgirl, who he has fallen in love with.
When the detective's dog does not make it into the final of the kennel club's dog show, fellow competitor the collector is disappointed, having hoped to savor a victory over the detective.
The next morning, the collector is found dead, inside his locked bedroom.
The district attorney and the police sergeant assume it was suicide because the collector was found holding a pistol.
The detective is not convinced, and foregoes a trip to a foreign country.
He soon finds bloodstain evidence that suggests the collector was murdered.
The coroner later determines the victim had bled to death internally from a stab wound.
There is no shortage of suspects; the collector was very much disliked.
His niece the young woman resented her uncle's tight control of her finances and jealousy of any men who showed interest in her.
Her boyfriend, the nobleman, suspected the collector of killing his dog to ensure winning the competition.

The suitor, the dead man's secretary, was in love with the young woman, but had been laughed at when he sought the collector's support, and heartbroken when the young woman informed him of her engagement to the nobleman.
The collector's next-door neighbor and lover the mistress had been cheating on him with the museum agent.
When the collector found out, he cancelled a contract to sell his vast collection of Chinese artworks to the foreign museum for which the museum agent worked.
The helper, the cook, had worked long, hard, and illegally to help the collector amass his collection.
He warned his employer against the proposed sale, but was angrily dismissed for eavesdropping.
Even the collector's own brother, the sibling, despised him, for reasons unknown.
Finally, the butler, the head servant, had concealed his criminal past.
The sibling becomes the detective's prime suspect, as his alibi of taking a train at the time of the murder is disproved.
However, when the sibling is found dead in a closet, the detective is both puzzled and enlightened.

Among the sibling's effects, the detective finds a book titled the true-crime book; a bookmarked page details a method of using string and fishing tackle to lock a door through the keyhole without leaving a trace.
The detective demonstrates this method for the district attorney and the police sergeant.
Later, an attempt is made on the life of the nobleman in his own bedroom; the attacker wields the same dagger used to kill the collector.
Finally, a Doberman Pinscher belonging to the mistress is found seriously injured in the collector's library, apparently struck with a fireside poker.
The detective solves the case, determining that two men sought to end the collector's life that night.
The successful murderer struggled with the collector and stabbed him, leaving him for dead.
The collector awakened soon after.
Too dazed to recall the fight or realize that he was mortally wounded, he went upstairs to his bedroom, opened his window, and began changing into his pajamas before dying.
A gloved sibling later entered the chamber; seeing his brother apparently asleep in his chair, he shot the corpse and arranged the scene to look like a suicide.
Downstairs, he ran into the actual killer, who had seen through a next-door window that the collector was still alive and come back to finish the job.
In the darkness, the killer mistook the sibling for the collector and killed the wrong man.
The dog then came in, attracted by the commotion, and attacked the murderer.
While sure of the killer's identity, the detective has no proof.
He therefore arranges for the nobleman and the suitor to quarrel over the young woman at the collector's residence.
The suitor antagonizes the couple's resolve to get married and moves to grab the nobleman, who sucker punches him.
When the suitor instinctively reaches for the poker to strike his rival, the Doberman recognizes its attacker and leaps on him.

After the detective pulls the dog away, the suitor confesses that the collector struck him after refusing to assist in his courtship of the young woman, precipitating the struggle and subsequent stabbing.
The attorney is defending his friend, the defendant, who has been charged with the murder of his wife the victim in the city.
By the defendant's account, the victim was unfaithful to him during their marriage.
After a court hearing, the attorney returns home to his wife, the spouse, and watches her as she applies make-up at her vanity.
The scene reminds him of the one the defendant described leading up to the victim's murder.
When the attorney attempts to kiss the spouse, she rebuffs him, criticizing him for ruining her make-up.
She then leaves their home.
The attorney follows the spouse through the streets of the city, and observes her meeting with a male lover.

This enrages the attorney, and he fantasizes about murdering the spouse; he also becomes obsessed with vindicating the defendant of killing the victim, hoping to prove in court that the defendant's extreme love for her drove him to a crime of passion.
Despite the parallels between the circumstances of the victim's murder and the spouse's current liaison, she still continues to visit her lover.
The attorney insists that the spouse be present during the final day of deliberations in the defendant's trial.
He makes an impassioned closing statement, which he concludes by revealing a gun and pointing it at the spouse in the audience.
She screams in horror and loses consciousness, after which the attorney finishes his speech.
While the jury deliberates, the attorney meets the spouse in his office, where she reacts in terror.
She insists she still loves him despite her affair.
The defendant is ultimately acquitted, and warns the attorney against killing the spouse, which he says he will regret.
The attorney heeds his advice, and asks the spouse to leave the courthouse.
Upon returning home, the attorney angrily smashes the spouse's vanity mirror.
The spouse appears behind him, and the two embrace.
In a foreign country, the home country's foreign ministry employee the investigator is caught trying to steal French state papers.
The investigator is released from his job and is deported.
Back in the home country, the investigator finds difficulty finding another job during the Great Depression.
He convinces the partner, a crooked and incompetent private detective, to become his partner.
Without the investigator's knowledge, the partner is financed by gangster the gambling boss and business booms.

The gambling boss complains that society woman the socialite is winning too much at his gambling tables and then hires the partner to uncover some sort of scandal that he can use to prevent the socialite from collecting her winnings.
The partner engages the investigator without telling him the true purpose of the request.
While keeping an eye on the socialite, the investigator falls in love with her.

When the socialite informs the gambling boss that she wants to collect her winnings, the partner suggests to the gambling boss that they fool the socialite into thinking that she has killed the gambling boss under suspicious conditions.
The partner double-crosses the gambling boss by hiring a thug to shoot him after the socialite leaves the apartment.
The socialite seeks the investigator's assistance.
The investigator learns the identity of the gambling boss's actual killer and traces him back to the partner.
Meanwhile, the partner tries to blackmail the socialite.
After the investigator has the partner arrested, he is offered his old job again, but tells the socialite that it is not the sort of life that he could ask anyone to share with him, so he leaves.
As he is departing, the socialite proposes marriage to him and he accepts.
